meta.blurb: Omar is fifty-two and wants more than a long life: he wants a good one. Over a year of walks up Bell Hill, his sister Salma shows him what really helps people stay strong, sharp and independent, and what is only hype.
meta.bible: Omar: a teacher who turns fifty-two at the start of the story; friendly, a little out of shape, and a grandfather. Salma: his younger sister, a Physiotherapist who loves numbers and hates hype; calm, funny and exact. Bell Hill: the hill with a long flight of stone steps where they walk once a month for a year, from one birthday to the next. Lifespan: the number of years a person lives. Healthspan: the number of those years lived in good health. Stamina, Strength, Balance, Flexibility: the four parts of fitness in this book. World Health Organization: advises adults to do at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, or half that of vigorous activity, and muscle-strengthening on at least two days a week. Dementia, Apnoea, Cholesterol, LDL, Osteoporosis, Screening, Physiotherapist, Dietitian: terms used with care. A large international review in 2024 estimated that up to forty-five percent of dementia cases might be prevented or delayed by tackling fourteen risk factors. Facts are hedged: studies often show links and not proof; no medicine or supplement has so far been proven to slow ageing in people; a simple plan beats an expensive one. Safety: people new to hard exercise, with a health condition, an injury or on medicine should ask a doctor first; chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain are signs to stop and get medical advice. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: warm, clear and practical, with a little humour; no invented numbers, studies or quotes; no diagnosis and no personal treatment advice.

B1B2: Omar turns fifty-two, and a friend's illness makes him wonder how to live a long and healthy life. His sister Salma, a physiotherapist, suggests a monthly walk up Bell Hill to talk about it.

Salma explains that lifespan is the number of years a person lives, while healthspan is the number of those years spent in good health. In many countries, people spend several of their last years living with illness.
Salma asks Omar to picture himself at eighty, and to say what he would still like to do. He answers that he wants to climb stairs, carry his shopping and play on the floor with his grandchildren.

Salma lists the big health problems of later life: heart and blood-vessel disease, cancer, type 2 diabetes and diseases of the brain such as dementia. Most of these are leading causes of death in rich countries, and injuries from falls also matter.
Most of these diseases build up slowly over decades, long before anyone feels ill. That is why the habits of today, in your forties and fifties, may matter more than they seem.
Salma compares our genes to a hand of cards dealt at birth. We cannot change the cards, she says, but the way we play them, through our daily habits, can make a big difference.
Salma says that a fit body has several parts: stamina, strength, balance and flexibility. Most people, she says, train one of them at most and forget the rest.
Stamina means how well your heart and lungs deliver oxygen during effort. Large studies show that fitter people tend to live longer, although fitter people may also differ from others in other ways.
The World Health Organization advises adults to do at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, such as brisk walking. You should breathe harder than usual, but still be able to talk.

Short bursts of hard effort, such as climbing stairs quickly, can improve fitness faster than steady walking alone. Salma warns that anyone new to hard exercise, or with a health condition, should ask a doctor first.
After about the age of thirty, most people slowly lose muscle mass unless they keep using it. The World Health Organization advises muscle-strengthening activities on at least two days a week.
Strong muscles let us climb stairs, lift bags and get up from the floor. They also help to protect the joints and bones, and they take up blood sugar, which is good for general health.

Salma asks Omar to squeeze a grip tester, and to stand up from a chair five times as fast as he can. In large studies, weak grip strength has been linked with poorer health later on, but it is a clue and not a diagnosis.

Bones are living tissue that grows stronger when it is loaded with weight, as it is by walking, lifting and carrying. Calcium, vitamin D and enough protein also help, and people worried about weak bones should ask a doctor.

Falls are one of the most common causes of serious injury in older people. Salma teaches Omar to stand on one leg beside a kitchen counter, holding on at first, and to practise it while the kettle boils.
Joints that are moved through their full range stay easier to use. Gentle stretching, yoga or simply reaching, squatting and turning during the day all help, though nobody needs to touch their toes.
Salma tells Omar to start slowly and to add a little more each week. Aching muscles are normal, but sharp pain, dizziness or chest pain are signs to stop and get medical advice.

Studies suggest that people who sit for many hours a day have a higher risk of poor health, especially if they also do little exercise. Salma advises Omar to stand up and move for a minute or two every half hour.
Health benefits grow with the number of daily steps, and for many people they level off at around seven to ten thousand. The famous ten thousand is a round number, not a magic one.
Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep a night. Over the years, short or poor sleep has been linked with a higher risk of heart disease, diabetes, accidents and low mood.
Good sleep habits include regular bed and wake times, a dark and cool bedroom, and daylight in the morning. Late coffee, big evening meals and bright screens can all make it harder to fall asleep.
Loud snoring with pauses in breathing, or great tiredness every day, can be signs of a sleep problem such as sleep apnoea. A doctor can check this, and treatment is often effective.

Salma's food advice is plain: eat mostly whole foods such as vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains and fish, and less of the processed kind. She says that keeping to the pattern for years matters more than any small detail.
Protein helps the body to keep and repair its muscles, and some experts think older people need a little more of it. People with kidney disease should ask a doctor before changing how much they eat.

Extra fat around the waist, deep inside the belly, is linked with a higher risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes. Salma measures Omar's waist, and explains that the number is only one clue among many.

Over many years, high blood sugar can damage blood vessels, nerves, eyes and kidneys, and type 2 diabetes is common in later life. A simple blood test can show whether sugar levels are normal, so Salma tells Omar to ask his doctor.

High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, yet over the years it raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney problems. It is easy to measure, and it can be treated, so regular checks are worth having.
Some kinds of cholesterol, especially LDL, can build up in the walls of blood vessels over many years. A blood test shows the level, and a doctor can explain what it means for each person.

Many countries invite people to cancer screening tests for the breast, the cervix and the bowel, depending on age. Salma tells Omar to accept the invitations, since finding a disease early often makes it easier to treat.
Not smoking is one of the best things anyone can do for their health, and quitting helps at any age. Alcohol is linked with several cancers and other diseases, so for health, less is better.

A large review in 2024 estimated that up to forty-five percent of dementia cases might be delayed or prevented by tackling fourteen risk factors. They include high blood pressure, poor hearing, smoking and loneliness.

Learning a language or an instrument keeps the brain active, and a lifetime of mental activity is linked with a lower risk of dementia. Brain-training apps, however, have so far shown much weaker evidence than real learning.

Studies link loneliness and social isolation with a higher risk of early death, heart disease and dementia. Close friendships and a sense of belonging, on the other hand, are linked with better health.

Everyone feels stress, but when it never stops it can harm sleep, mood and the body. Salma says that exercise, time outdoors, friends, and talking to a professional when needed are all useful ways to cope.

Several studies link a strong sense of purpose, such as caring for others or working on a project, with a longer and healthier life. The link probably goes both ways, since healthier people also find it easier to be active.

Untreated hearing loss is linked with a higher risk of dementia, and poor eyesight raises the risk of falls. Regular hearing and eye checks are therefore a simple and useful part of any long-term plan.
Not every risk comes from a slow disease, and some can be avoided with very little effort. Seat belts, helmets, sun protection and recommended vaccines for older adults all prevent harm.
Salma suggests a simple notebook: how far he walks, how much he can lift, how well he sleeps. She warns that numbers are only a guide, and that more and more testing is not always better.
Shops and websites sell pills and powders that promise to slow ageing. So far, no supplement or medicine has been proven to do this in people, so Salma advises being careful with such claims.

Scientists are studying ways to slow ageing, including certain medicines and special eating patterns. Most of this work so far has been done on animals or in small human studies, so the results are still uncertain.
Salma advises tying a new habit to an old one, such as stretching while the kettle boils or walking after dinner. Small, regular actions, she says, last much longer than big plans.
Omar joins a walking group, and he finds that it is easier to keep going when friends expect him. Salma smiles, because she says that company is often the best motivation.
In summer, Omar twists his ankle and stops walking for several weeks. Salma tells him that setbacks happen to everyone, and that the important thing is to restart gently as soon as it is safe.

People start from very different places, with different ages, abilities and health conditions. Almost anyone can find movement that suits them, such as chair exercises, swimming or short walks, and a doctor or physiotherapist can help.
A long-life plan does not need a gym, special gadgets or expensive supplements. Walking, climbing stairs, simple strength exercises at home, good sleep and cheap whole foods can do most of the work.

In their thirties and forties, people build habits and fitness. In their fifties and sixties, keeping muscle and bone becomes especially important, and in their seventies and beyond, balance and independence become the priorities.

After a year of walks, Omar climbs all the steps of Bell Hill without stopping, and he can stand up from the floor easily. He does not know how many extra years he has gained, because nobody can know that.
Salma reminds Omar that no plan can promise a long life, because luck and genes also play their part. What a good plan can do is improve the odds and make the years ahead more comfortable.
Salma writes the whole plan on one page: move, lift, sleep well, eat whole foods, keep friends close, and have regular check-ups. Omar sticks it on the fridge, next to a drawing by his granddaughter.

This book gives general information about living longer and healthier, and it is not medical advice. Please talk to a doctor before starting hard exercise or making big changes, especially if you have a health condition.
C1C2: When Omar turned fifty-two, a close friend fell seriously ill, and the news set him wondering how a person might live not merely long but well. His sister Salma, a physiotherapist who loved numbers and hated hype, proposed a bargain: one walk a month up the steps of Bell Hill, with one question answered at each stop. Omar, who had never climbed the hill without stopping for breath, agreed at once.

Salma begins with two words: lifespan, the number of years a person lives, and healthspan, the number of those years lived in good health. Life expectancy has risen enormously over the past century, she notes, but in many countries people now spend several of their last years with illness or disability. The aim, she says, is not simply more birthdays but more years in which a person can walk, think, work and laugh as they please.

Salma asks her brother to picture himself at eighty and to describe, in concrete detail, what he hopes still to be doing. Omar, after some thought, answers that he wants to climb stairs without a rail, carry his own shopping, travel with his family and get up from the floor after playing with his grandchildren. These are the goals, she says, from which every sensible plan must start, because training for them in your fifties is far easier than trying to recover them in your eighties.

Salma sketches the main threats to a long and healthy life: diseases of the heart and blood vessels, cancers, type 2 diabetes and diseases of the brain such as dementia. Together with injuries from falls and accidents, these account for a large share of illness and early death in rich countries, although the exact picture differs from place to place. They sound alarming, she says, but they have something hopeful in common, which is that they develop slowly and respond to habits.

Most of these diseases, Salma explains, develop silently over many years, so that the narrowing of an artery or the loss of muscle may begin decades before anyone notices a symptom. By the time a problem announces itself, a great deal of damage may already have been done, and the choices are fewer. That is why the habits of the forties and fifties, though they feel invisible, may be among the most valuable investments a person can make.

Salma compares our genes to a hand of cards dealt at birth: nobody chooses it, and some hands are plainly kinder than others. Yet the way the cards are played, through everyday habits of movement, sleep, food and friendship, can change the odds considerably, and many families with a history of illness have seen the pattern broken. No habit gives a guarantee, she is careful to add, and bad luck can strike the best-prepared person.

A fit body, Salma says, has four parts that work together: stamina, which is the endurance of the heart and lungs; strength, the power of the muscles; balance, the ability to stay steady; and flexibility, the freedom of the joints. Most people train one of these at best, usually the one they already enjoy, and neglect the other three. Her plan for Omar will touch all four, but it will begin with the one that predicts the most.

Stamina, Salma explains, is the capacity of the heart, lungs and muscles to deliver and use oxygen during effort, and it is one of the best measures of general fitness that researchers have. Large studies have found that people with higher fitness tend to live longer than people with low fitness, and the difference is bigger than that for many well-known risk factors. As always, she adds, such findings show a strong link and not a proof, since healthier people find it easier to be fit.

The World Health Organization advises adults to aim for at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, such as brisk walking, or half that amount of vigorous activity. A simple test, Salma says, is the talk test: during moderate effort you breathe harder but can still hold a conversation, while during vigorous effort you can manage only a few words. Omar discovers that his usual stroll fails the test, since he could happily sing, but his brisk walk with Salma passes it.

Short bursts of hard effort, such as climbing stairs briskly or cycling up a slope, can raise fitness faster than steady walking alone, which suits busy people who cannot spare an hour. Salma insists, however, that anyone who is new to hard exercise, over a certain age, or living with a health condition should speak to a doctor before trying it. Omar, who has promised to do so, decides to begin with a single fast flight of steps and a long rest.

From about the age of thirty, Salma explains, most people slowly lose muscle mass, and the loss tends to speed up in later decades unless the muscles are given work to do. The World Health Organization therefore advises adults to include muscle-strengthening activities on at least two days a week, whether with weights, resistance bands, machines or simply the weight of their own bodies. Omar, who has never lifted anything heavier than a suitcase, listens with a growing sense of obligation.

Strong muscles, Salma says, are not about appearance but about independence, since they decide whether a person can rise from a chair, climb a flight of stairs, lift a bag or recover from a stumble. They also help to protect the joints and bones, and they take up sugar from the blood, which helps the body to manage its energy. Muscle is therefore less a luxury for the young than a kind of savings account for the old.

To give him a starting point, Salma asks Omar to squeeze a hand grip as hard as he can and to rise from a chair five times in a row without using his arms. Weak grip strength has been linked in large studies with poorer health and a higher risk of early death, she says, although it is a clue and not a diagnosis, and it can be improved with training. Omar's numbers are average, which is neither shameful nor remarkable, and he feels strangely relieved to know them.

Bones, Salma tells him, are living tissue, and like muscles they respond to the work they are given: walking, climbing, lifting and carrying all encourage them to stay dense. Enough calcium, vitamin D and protein also help, while smoking and heavy drinking work in the opposite direction. Osteoporosis, the thinning of the bones, can lead to fractures after small falls, so anyone who is worried about their bones, she adds, should ask a doctor about a check.

Falls, Salma explains, are one of the commonest causes of serious injury in older people, and a broken hip can change a life overnight. Balance is a skill that can be trained, and reviews of the research have found that exercise programmes with balance training, including tai chi, reduce the rate of falls. She teaches Omar to stand on one leg beside the kitchen counter, holding on at first, and to practise every day while the kettle boils.

Joints that are moved through their full range of motion tend to stay easier to use, while those that are never stretched slowly stiffen, which is why flexibility belongs on the list. Gentle stretching, yoga, swimming or simply reaching, squatting and turning during the day can all help, and nobody, Salma jokes, needs to be able to touch their toes. What matters is that Omar can put on his socks, look over his shoulder when he parks a car and reach the top shelf without pain.

The most important rule, Salma tells him, is to begin gently and to add a little more each week, since the people who injure themselves are usually the ones who try to make up for decades in a fortnight. Aching muscles the day after exercise are normal, but sharp pain, dizziness, unusual breathlessness or chest pain are signals to stop at once and to seek medical advice. Good technique matters more than heavy weights, she adds, and a session or two with a qualified trainer is money well spent.

Studies suggest that people who sit for most of the day have a higher risk of heart disease, diabetes and early death, especially when they also take little exercise. Omar, who marks essays for hours at a stretch, recognises himself at once, but Salma does not ask him to give up his desk, only to stand up and move for a minute or two every half hour. A short walk to the window, a few squats or a stretch beside the chair, she says, is enough to interrupt the long stillness.

Many studies suggest that the health benefits of walking grow with the number of daily steps, and that for many people they begin to level off somewhere between about seven thousand and ten thousand. The famous target of ten thousand, Salma says, began life as a round number in an advertising campaign, and there is nothing magical about it. Whatever Omar's number is today, she tells him, the best goal is a few hundred more than that, and the benefits come even at modest levels.

Most adults, Salma explains, need between seven and nine hours of sleep a night, and the brain and body use that time to repair themselves, to store memories and to regulate hunger and mood. Short or poor sleep over many years has been linked with a higher risk of heart disease, diabetes, accidents and low mood, although the exact reasons are still being studied. Omar, who regularly sleeps six hours and boasts about it, is told with some tact that he is not as unaffected as he believes.

Good sleep, Salma says, is helped by regular bed and wake times, a bedroom that is dark, quiet and cool, and a good dose of daylight in the morning, which anchors the body's clock. Late coffee, heavy evening meals, alcohol and bright screens can all disturb it, so Omar agrees to leave his phone to charge in the hallway. After a few weeks, he is surprised to find that he is falling asleep faster and waking before the alarm.

Loud, regular snoring with pauses in breathing, or heavy tiredness during the day despite a full night in bed, can be a sign of a sleep disorder such as sleep apnoea, in which the airway repeatedly narrows during sleep. Salma cannot diagnose it, she says, and neither can a diary, but a doctor can arrange simple tests, and effective treatments exist. It is a good example of a problem that is easy to ignore and well worth the trouble of finding.

Salma's advice about food is deliberately plain: eat mostly whole foods such as vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, nuts and fish, eat less of the highly processed kind, and keep an eye on portion size. The details of the perfect diet are still argued over by researchers, she admits, but the broad pattern has stayed the same for decades and is not controversial. What matters most, she says, is not a clever rule but the habit that a person can keep for twenty years.

Protein supplies the building blocks that the body uses to maintain and repair its muscles, and some experts suggest that older adults need rather more of it than the young, partly because ageing muscles respond less well to it. Beans, lentils, fish, eggs, dairy foods, tofu and nuts are all good sources, and a little at each meal works better than a lot at one. People with kidney disease, Salma warns, are sometimes told to limit protein, so they should take advice before changing what they eat.

Fat that collects deep inside the belly is linked more strongly with heart disease and type 2 diabetes than fat stored elsewhere, so Salma measures Omar's waist with a soft tape. Many health bodies suggest that a waist measurement of less than half a person's height is a useful rough guide. She stresses, however, that it is only one clue among many, and Omar, who is slightly over the line, resolves to take it as information rather than as an insult.

Over many years, blood sugar that stays too high can damage the blood vessels, nerves, eyes and kidneys, and type 2 diabetes becomes more common with age, particularly in people who are inactive or carry extra weight around the middle. A simple blood test can show whether a person's sugar levels are in the normal range, and early signs can often be reversed or controlled with changes in habits. Salma tells Omar that this is a question for his doctor, who can decide how often to test him.

High blood pressure, Salma says, is often called the silent condition, since it usually causes no symptoms at all while it quietly strains the arteries, the heart, the brain and the kidneys over the years. It is easy to measure, in a clinic, a pharmacy or at home, and when it is high there are many effective ways to lower it, from less salt and more exercise to medicine from a doctor. Omar, who has not had his blood pressure taken for six years, makes an appointment on his phone before they reach the next bench.

Cholesterol is a fatty substance that the body needs in small amounts, but certain forms of it, particularly the one known as LDL, can build up in the walls of arteries over many years and narrow them. Salma draws a pipe on her notepad, furred with deposits, as a crude but useful picture of the process. A blood test shows a person's levels, and a doctor can explain what they mean in the light of age, family history and other risks, and whether treatment would help.

Many countries invite people to take part in screening programmes, which look for certain cancers, such as those of the breast, the cervix and the bowel, before they cause symptoms. Salma explains that finding a disease early often makes it easier to treat, though no test is perfect, and each has small risks that a doctor can discuss. Her advice to Omar is to find out which tests are offered where he lives and when, and then to accept the invitations.

Not smoking, Salma says, is among the most powerful things that anyone can do for their health, and quitting brings benefits at any age, even after decades of the habit, and a doctor can help. Alcohol is also linked with several cancers, liver disease and accidents, and most health bodies now say that for health the less a person drinks, the better. Omar, who enjoys one glass of wine on Fridays, decides that he can live with this advice.

Salma tells him that a large international review published in 2024 estimated that up to forty-five percent of dementia cases worldwide might be delayed or prevented by tackling fourteen known risk factors. These include high blood pressure, hearing loss, smoking, inactivity, heavy drinking and loneliness, although the figure is an estimate and not a promise, and nobody can guarantee that any one person will escape the disease. Yet it is encouraging that so many of the factors lie, at least partly, within reach.

Learning a language, a musical instrument or any demanding new skill keeps the brain active, and more years of education and mentally stimulating work are linked with a lower risk of dementia. It is hard to separate the effect of the mind from that of the lifestyle that goes with it, however, and the evidence for commercial brain-training games is much weaker, Salma says. Omar decides to learn some Spanish, and begins by ordering coffee in it, since real learning, with its struggles and small triumphs, seems the safer bet.

Studies in many countries link loneliness and social isolation with a higher risk of early death, heart disease and dementia, and the effect seems comparable to that of some well-known habits such as smoking. Close friendships, family ties and a sense of belonging, on the other hand, are linked with better health and a longer life, though it is not always easy to tell which causes which. Salma, who has seen lonely patients recover more slowly than those with visitors, regards friendship as part of a serious plan.

Everyone meets stress, Salma says, and in short bursts it can even help, but stress that never lets up can disturb sleep, lower the mood and strain the body. Exercise, time outdoors, friends, hobbies, quiet moments and, when needed, talking to a doctor or a trained counsellor are all sensible ways of coping, and asking for help is a sign of good sense and not of weakness. She and Omar spend ten minutes on the hilltop saying nothing at all, and Omar finds that it is surprisingly hard.

Several studies have linked a strong sense of purpose, whether it comes from family, work, a cause, a craft or simply caring for a garden, with a longer and healthier life. The link probably runs in both directions, Salma admits, since healthier people also find it easier to pursue goals, but she thinks that a reason to get up in the morning is worth cultivating either way. Omar, who has recently become a volunteer reader at a primary school, finds that he agrees.

Hearing loss that is left untreated is one of the risk factors linked with dementia, perhaps because it isolates people or because the brain must work harder to understand speech, while poor eyesight increases the risk of falls and accidents. Regular hearing and eye tests are therefore a modest and useful part of any long-term plan, Salma says, and hearing aids and glasses are much better and cheaper than they were. Omar takes a hearing test, and is told, to his wife's amusement, that he is not selectively deaf after all.

Not every risk to a long life comes from a slow disease, Salma points out, and some of the cheapest protections are also the most overlooked. Seat belts, cycle helmets, sunscreen and shade, working smoke alarms and the vaccines that health services recommend for older adults, such as those against influenza, all prevent harm for very little effort. The best plans, she says, include the dull things that quietly stop bad things from happening.

Salma suggests that Omar keep a simple notebook in which he records how far he walks, how much he can lift, how well he sleeps and how he feels. Progress that is written down, she says, is much harder to forget or deny, but she warns him that numbers are guides and not masters, and that endless testing can cause needless worry without improving anyone's health. Medical tests, she says, are best chosen with a doctor who knows the person and the evidence.

Shops and websites are full of pills, powders and injections that promise to slow ageing or to turn back the clock, usually at a high price and supported by a few impressive-sounding words. So far, Salma tells Omar, no supplement or medicine has been proven to slow ageing in people, and the glowing stories are often based on animal experiments or on very small studies. Before spending money on any such product, she suggests, he should ask whether the evidence would convince a careful doctor.

That does not mean that the science of ageing is empty, Salma adds, since researchers around the world are studying medicines, eating patterns and many other ideas that might slow the biology of ageing. Most of this work is still at an early stage, based on animals or on small and short studies in people, and a promising result in a laboratory often fails to hold up in a large trial. She follows the field with interest, but she would not bet a year of her health on any of it.

Habits are easiest to build, Salma says, when they are attached to something that already happens every day, so Omar practises standing on one leg while the kettle boils and puts on his walking shoes immediately after breakfast. Small, regular actions last much longer than heroic plans, which usually collapse in the second week, and the secret is to make the first step so easy that it is difficult to refuse. Within a month, the new routine no longer feels like a decision at all.

In the spring, Omar joins a Saturday walking group of neighbours, and he discovers that it is far easier to turn up when other people are waiting for him than when the only witness is his own conscience. Salma, who has long believed that company is the most underrated form of motivation, is delighted. The group walks, talks and drinks tea afterwards, and nobody mentions heart rates or distances at all.

In summer, Omar twists his ankle on a loose stone and has to rest for several weeks, and he is miserable at the thought that all his progress will vanish. Salma reassures him that setbacks happen to everyone, through illness, injury, travel or simple busyness, and that the important thing is to restart gently as soon as it is safe, ideally after advice from a doctor or physiotherapist. A plan that cannot survive an interruption, she says, was never a plan but a performance.

Not everyone begins from the same place, Salma reminds him, since people differ in age, ability, injury, illness and the time and money that they have to spend. Almost anyone can find some kind of movement that suits them, whether chair exercises, swimming, gentle stretching, walking aids or short walks several times a day, and a doctor or physiotherapist can help to plan it safely. The only wrong starting point, she says, is the one that is chosen by comparing oneself with somebody else.

A long-life plan, Salma insists, does not require a gym membership, a smartwatch with a dozen dials or a cupboard full of expensive supplements, although any of these may be useful for somebody. Walking, climbing stairs, simple strength exercises at home, regular sleep, friends and cheap whole foods such as beans, oats and vegetables can do most of the work. The most valuable item of all, she says, is consistency, and it is entirely free, which makes it the best bargain on the whole list.

Each stage of life, Salma suggests, has its own emphasis: the thirties and forties are for building habits and fitness, the fifties and sixties for keeping muscle and bone, and the seventies and beyond for balance and independence. It is never too early to begin and never too late, she says, because studies show that even people who start exercising in later life gain real benefits. Walking up the hill that day, they pass a woman of eighty-three with a stick and a shopping bag, who greets them with a cheerful nod.

On the last walk of the year, Omar climbs every step of Bell Hill without stopping, and he reaches the top with a pink face, steady breathing and a grin that he cannot hide. He can now rise from the floor with ease, his blood pressure and sleep are better, and his granddaughter says that he is much faster at chasing her. How many extra years he has gained, nobody can say, but he is quite sure that the years he has will be better ones.

Salma reminds her brother that no plan can promise a long life, since luck and genes will always play a part, and that anyone who sells certainty is selling something else. What a good plan can do is to improve the odds, to delay or soften the diseases that come with age, and to make the years ahead more comfortable, active and free. That, she says, is a sensible and honest ambition, and it happens to be a pleasant one to pursue.

Salma writes the whole plan on a single sheet of paper: move most days, lift something heavy, practise balance, sleep well, eat whole foods, keep friends close, avoid tobacco and have regular check-ups. Omar reads it twice and observes that it is not very exciting, and Salma replies that this is exactly its strength. He sticks it to the fridge, beside a drawing by his granddaughter, where it stays for years.

Omar and Salma sit on the top step as the sun sinks behind the hills and agree that the best plan is the one you will truly keep, one gentle step after another. This book offers general information only and is not medical advice, so please consult a doctor or another health professional about your own needs, tests and treatments. For now, the next step is small and simple: put on your shoes, and go out for a walk.
